API1.name: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA)
API1.description: APIs tend to expose endpoints that handle object identifiers, creating a wide attack surface of Object Level Access Control issues. Object level authorization checks should be considered in every function that accesses a data source using an input from the user.
API1.impact: Attackers can read, modify, or delete other users' data by simply changing the object ID in requests. This leads to unauthorized data access, privacy violations, and potential financial fraud.

remediation.summary: Implement proper object-level authorization on every endpoint that accesses data using user-supplied IDs.
steps: Implement authorization checks on every API endpoint that accesses a data source using user-provided IDs
Use server-side policies to verify that the requesting user has permission to access the requested object
Replace sequential integer IDs with random, non-guessable UUIDs (e.g., UUID v4)
Never trust client-supplied object IDs — always validate ownership on the server
Log unauthorized access attempts and alert on anomalous patterns
Write automated tests to verify authorization for every endpoint

code_example.vulnerable:
# VULNERABLE: No ownership check
@app.get('/api/orders/{order_id}')
async def get_order(order_id: int, token: str):
    user = decode_token(token)
    order = db.get_order(order_id)  # Returns ANY order!
    return order
code_example.secure:
# SECURE: Ownership verified
@app.get('/api/orders/{order_id}')
async def get_order(order_id: int, token: str):
    user = decode_token(token)
    order = db.get_order(order_id)
    if order.user_id != user.id:  # Verify ownership!
        raise HTTPException(403, 'Forbidden')
    return order

API2.name: Broken Authentication
API2.description: Authentication mechanisms are often implemented incorrectly, allowing attackers to compromise authentication tokens or exploit implementation flaws to assume other users' identities temporarily or permanently.
API2.impact: Full account takeover, unauthorized access to sensitive data, privilege escalation. A single compromised admin account can expose the entire system.

remediation.summary: Implement strong authentication with proper token validation, expiry, and brute-force protection.
steps: Always verify JWT signatures using strong algorithms (RS256 or HS256) — never accept 'none' algorithm
Set short token expiry times (15-60 minutes for access tokens)
Implement refresh token rotation — invalidate old refresh tokens when new ones are issued
Add rate limiting and account lockout on login endpoints (e.g., 5 attempts → 15-minute lockout)
Implement multi-factor authentication (MFA) for sensitive operations
Never log or expose authentication tokens in URLs or error messages
Use HTTPS everywhere — never send credentials over HTTP
Invalidate tokens server-side on logout (use a token blocklist)

code_example.vulnerable:
# VULNERABLE: Accepts 'none' algorithm, no expiry check
def verify_token(token):
    decoded = jwt.decode(token, options={'verify_signature': False})
    return decoded

API3.name: Broken Object Property Level Authorization
API3.description: This category combines Excessive Data Exposure and Mass Assignment. APIs may expose more data than necessary, or blindly bind client-provided data to internal objects, allowing attackers to access confidential properties or escalate privileges.
API3.impact: Attackers can escalate privileges (e.g., make themselves admin), expose sensitive PII, or manipulate financial data by including unauthorized fields in requests.

remediation.summary: Use explicit allowlists for bindable properties and never expose more data than needed.
steps: Never automatically bind all request parameters to model objects — use explicit allowlists
Define separate request/response schemas — input schema only allows safe fields
Mark sensitive fields as write-protected or read-only at the model level
Return only the minimum data needed by the client — use response DTOs
Never return password hashes, internal IDs, audit fields, or security flags in responses
Validate that the requesting user has permission to set each provided field

code_example.vulnerable:
# VULNERABLE: All fields from request bound to model
@app.post('/api/users')
async def create_user(user_data: dict):
    user = User(**user_data)  # isAdmin, role etc. all accepted!
    db.save(user)
code_example.secure:
# SECURE: Explicit allowlist using Pydantic schema
class CreateUserRequest(BaseModel):
    username: str
    email: str
    password: str
    # isAdmin, role, etc. NOT included — cannot be set by client

@app.post('/api/users')
async def create_user(user_data: CreateUserRequest):
    user = User(
        username=user_data.username,
        email=user_data.email,
        password=hash(user_data.password),
        is_admin=False,  # Always set server-side
        role='user'      # Always set server-side
    )
    db.save(user)

API4.name: Unrestricted Resource Consumption
API4.description: Satisfying API requests requires resources such as network bandwidth, CPU, memory, and storage. Lack of rate limiting or resource controls allows attackers to abuse APIs for DoS attacks or to cause excessive costs.
API4.impact: Denial of Service (DoS), financial damage from cloud resource costs, slow response times for legitimate users, brute-force attacks enabled by no throttling.

remediation.summary: Implement rate limiting, request size limits, and resource quotas at the API gateway level.
steps: Implement rate limiting per IP, user, and API key (e.g., 100 requests/minute per user)
Return HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests) with Retry-After header when limits are exceeded
Limit maximum request body size (e.g., 1MB) and reject larger payloads with 413
Set timeouts on all database queries and external service calls
Paginate all list endpoints — never return unlimited results
Monitor resource usage and alert on anomalous consumption patterns
Implement exponential backoff requirements for repeated failed requests

code_example.vulnerable:
# VULNERABLE: No rate limiting
@app.get('/api/users')
async def get_users():
    return db.get_all_users()  # Returns millions of records!

API5.name: Broken Function Level Authorization
API5.description: Complex access control policies with different hierarchies, groups, and roles, combined with unclear separation between administrative and regular functions, tend to lead to authorization flaws.
API5.impact: Attackers can access administrative or privileged functions, allowing them to delete users, modify system settings, access other users' data at scale, or take over the entire application.

remediation.summary: Deny all access by default and explicitly grant permissions based on user roles.
steps: Default deny: block all access unless explicitly granted
Implement Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) or Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC)
Move all admin functions to a separate API prefix (/admin/) and protect with role middleware
Validate the user's role on every request — never trust client-provided roles
Do not expose admin functionality based on hidden UI — attackers will find it
Audit all HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) on every endpoint for each role
Regularly review which users have admin privileges

code_example.vulnerable:
# VULNERABLE: No role check
@app.delete('/api/admin/users/{user_id}')
async def delete_user(user_id: int, token: str):
    user = decode_token(token)  # Doesn't check if admin!
    db.delete_user(user_id)

API6.name: Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows
API6.description: APIs vulnerable to this risk expose a business flow — such as buying a ticket, or posting a comment — without compensating for how the functionality could harm the business if used excessively in an automated fashion.
API6.impact: Mass coupon fraud, ticket scalping bots, inventory manipulation, fake account creation at scale, abuse of referral/reward systems, and denial of service to legitimate users.

remediation.summary: Identify and protect business-critical flows with device fingerprinting, CAPTCHA, and flow-specific rate limits.
steps: Identify all business-critical flows (checkout, OTP, coupon, voting, password reset)
Implement CAPTCHA or proof-of-work challenges on flows susceptible to bot abuse
Add per-user rate limits specifically for each business flow
Implement device fingerprinting to detect multiple accounts from same device
Monitor for unusual patterns (e.g., 100 coupon redemptions from single IP)
Use one-time tokens for sensitive operations (OTP should expire in 5 minutes)
Alert on anomalous usage patterns in real-time

code_example.vulnerable:
# VULNERABLE: No protection on coupon redemption
@app.post('/api/coupon/apply')
async def apply_coupon(code: str, user_id: int):
    coupon = db.get_coupon(code)
    db.apply_discount(user_id, coupon.discount)  # Can be called unlimited times!

API7.name: Server Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
API7.description: Server-Side Request Forgery flaws can occur when an API is fetching a remote resource without validating the user-supplied URL. This allows an attacker to coerce the application into sending a crafted request to an unexpected destination.
API7.impact: Access to internal services (databases, cloud metadata APIs), port scanning of internal network, data exfiltration, potential Remote Code Execution via internal services. AWS/GCP metadata APIs can expose cloud credentials.

remediation.summary: Validate and sanitize all user-supplied URLs using an allowlist of permitted domains.
steps: Never accept arbitrary URLs from users — use an allowlist of permitted domains/IPs
Validate URL scheme — only allow https:// and reject file://, ftp://, gopher://, dict://
Block requests to cloud metadata endpoints: 169.254.169.254, metadata.google.internal
Resolve DNS before validating (protect against DNS rebinding attacks)
Disable unnecessary URL-fetching features in your application
Run URL-fetching functionality in an isolated network segment with no internal access

code_example.vulnerable:
# VULNERABLE: Fetches any URL
@app.post('/api/fetch')
async def fetch_url(url: str):
    resp = requests.get(url)  # Attacker sets url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/
    return resp.text

API8.name: Security Misconfiguration
API8.description: APIs and the systems supporting them typically contain complex configurations that can be misconfigured. Missing security hardening, unnecessary features enabled, permissive CORS, and verbose error messages all constitute security misconfigurations.
API8.impact: Information leakage (stack traces, internal paths), cross-origin data theft via CORS misconfiguration, unauthorized access via exposed debug endpoints, and broader attack surface for further exploitation.

remediation.summary: Apply security hardening across all layers: disable debug features, configure CORS strictly, and add security headers.
steps: Remove all debug, test, and development endpoints from production
Configure CORS with an explicit allowlist — never use Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
Add all required security headers: Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options
Hide server version information (remove Server and X-Powered-By headers)
Return generic error messages — never expose stack traces to clients
Disable HTTP methods you don't use (TRACE, OPTIONS if not needed)
Keep all dependencies and frameworks up to date
Regularly audit configurations with automated tools (OWASP ZAP, nuclei)

code_example.vulnerable:
# VULNERABLE: Wildcard CORS + debug mode
app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=['*'],  # Any origin!
    allow_credentials=True,  # With credentials!
)
app = FastAPI(debug=True)  # Exposes stack traces
code_example.secure:
# SECURE: Strict CORS + no debug
ALLOWED_ORIGINS = ['https://myapp.com', 'https://app.myapp.com']
app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=ALLOWED_ORIGINS,
    allow_credentials=True,
    allow_methods=['GET', 'POST', 'PUT', 'DELETE'],
    allow_headers=['Authorization', 'Content-Type'],
)
app = FastAPI(debug=False)

@app.middleware('http')
async def add_security_headers(request, call_next):
    response = await call_next(request)
    response.headers['X-Frame-Options'] = 'DENY'
    response.headers['X-Content-Type-Options'] = 'nosniff'
    response.headers['Strict-Transport-Security'] = 'max-age=31536000'
    response.headers['Content-Security-Policy'] = "default-src 'self'"
    return response

API9.name: Improper Inventory Management
API9.description: APIs tend to expose more endpoints than traditional web applications. Proper documentation and an up-to-date inventory is extremely important. Old/deprecated API versions often lack the security controls of the current version.
API9.impact: Attackers find old API versions that bypass security controls added later, access undocumented internal endpoints, or exploit forgotten debug/test endpoints that were never removed from production.

remediation.summary: Maintain a complete API inventory and sunset deprecated versions with proper versioning strategy.
steps: Maintain an always up-to-date API inventory in your API gateway or documentation
Document all API versions, their deprecation dates, and the endpoints they expose
Formally deprecate and sunset old API versions — don't leave them running indefinitely
Apply the same security controls to all API versions — never have a 'secure v2' and 'insecure v1'
Use API gateways to enforce which endpoints are accessible in production
Scan for shadow APIs (undocumented endpoints) using tools like 42Crunch or Postman
Review third-party APIs your application depends on — they may expose your data

API10.name: Unsafe Consumption of APIs
API10.description: Developers tend to trust data received from third-party APIs more than user input. APIs that interact with third-party services may be vulnerable if the data from those services is not properly validated and sanitized before use.
API10.impact: Injection attacks via malicious third-party data, open redirect exploitation for phishing, credential harvesting via unvalidated redirects, and data integrity issues from unverified external sources.

remediation.summary: Treat all third-party API data as untrusted — validate, sanitize, and verify before use.
steps: Validate and sanitize ALL data received from third-party APIs — treat it as untrusted user input
Never pass third-party redirect URLs directly to users — validate against allowlist first
Use strict output encoding when rendering third-party data in responses
Interact with third-party APIs only over HTTPS — never over HTTP
Implement timeouts and circuit breakers for third-party API calls
Validate the schema/structure of third-party API responses before processing
Avoid passing sensitive user data to third-party APIs unless absolutely necessary

code_example.vulnerable:
# VULNERABLE: Third-party data used without validation
@app.get('/api/user-info')
async def get_user_info(user_id: str):
    # Third-party API may return malicious data
    third_party_data = await external_api.get_user(user_id)
    return third_party_data  # Returned as-is — may contain XSS, injection!
